What is Ionic and how does a hybrid app work?

Ionic is a UI toolkit of mobile-styled web components for building cross-platform apps with web technologies. A hybrid app is a web app (HTML/CSS/JS) packaged inside a native shell that renders it in a WebView; a native runtime (Capacitor) provides a bridge so JavaScript can call device APIs like the camera or GPS. One codebase targets Android, iOS and the web.
What is the difference between Capacitor and Cordova?

Both bridge web code to native APIs. Capacitor is the modern successor: native projects are committed source you open in Android Studio/Xcode, plugins use a Promise-based typed API, plugins can also work on the web, and writing custom native code is straightforward. Cordova regenerates native platforms from config and relies on an older plugin model. Capacitor can run most Cordova plugins, so migration is incremental. 💡 New Ionic projects use Capacitor by default.
Ionic vs React Native vs Flutter?

Ionic renders web components in a WebView, so it reuses web/Angular skills and code and also deploys as a PWA. React Native renders real native widgets driven by JavaScript; Flutter draws its own widgets with the Skia/Impeller engine using Dart. Ionic is fastest to adopt for web teams and great for business/form-driven apps; RN and Flutter can feel more native for heavy animation or graphics-intensive apps.
Why use ion-router-outlet instead of router-outlet?

ion-router-outlet keeps previously visited pages in a navigation stack instead of destroying them, enabling native page transition animations, swipe-to-go-back on iOS and preserved scroll position. It still uses Angular Router configuration underneath. The trade-off is that component lifecycle differs, so you rely on Ionic page lifecycle events.
What are Ionic page lifecycle hooks and why are they needed?

ionViewWillEnter, ionViewDidEnter, ionViewWillLeave and ionViewDidLeave. Because Ionic caches pages in the stack, ngOnInit runs only once when a page is first created and ngOnDestroy only when it is popped. To refresh data each time a user returns to a page (e.g. after editing a record on a detail page), load it in ionViewWillEnter.

What does npx cap sync do?

It runs cap copy (copies the built web assets from webDir into the native Android and iOS projects) and cap update (installs/updates native dependencies for Capacitor plugins, e.g. Gradle and CocoaPods/SPM). Run it after every web build you want to test natively and after adding or upgrading plugins.
How do you build and publish an Ionic app for Android and iOS?

Run ionic build (production Angular build), npx cap sync, then npx cap open android / ios. In Android Studio generate a signed AAB for Google Play; in Xcode configure signing with an Apple developer account and archive to upload to App Store Connect. iOS builds require macOS (or a cloud build service). Set the bundle ID via appId in capacitor.config.ts.
How does Ionic handle platform-specific styling?

Ionic applies a mode automatically — ios on Apple devices and md (Material) elsewhere — so the same component renders with platform-appropriate look and behaviour. You can force a mode globally via provideIonicAngular({ mode: 'ios' }) or per component with the mode attribute, target .ios/.md classes in CSS, and use the Platform service (platform.is('android')) in code.
How do you theme Ionic components?

Through CSS custom properties: global colours such as --ion-color-primary (with shade/tint/contrast variants) in variables.scss, and component-level variables like --background or --color. Because many components use Shadow DOM, normal selectors cannot reach internals — use the documented variables or ::part(). Ionic 8 ships dark mode palettes you can enable via class or system preference.
How do you store data locally in an Ionic app?

For small key-value settings use @capacitor/preferences (backed by SharedPreferences / UserDefaults). For larger structured or offline data use SQLite (via a community Capacitor SQLite plugin) or IndexedDB-based libraries such as Ionic Storage. Avoid relying on localStorage for important data on iOS, as the OS can clear WebView storage. Never store secrets like raw passwords; use secure storage plugins for tokens where required.
How do you call a Spring Boot backend from an Ionic app?

Exactly as in Angular — HttpClient in a service with interceptors for JWT headers and error handling. Points specific to mobile: the device cannot reach localhost, so use the machine's LAN IP or a deployed URL; configure CORS on the backend for the app's origin (capacitor://localhost on iOS, http://localhost on Android); and use HTTPS, since Android blocks cleartext by default. Capacitor's CapacitorHttp can route requests natively to bypass CORS.
How do you improve performance of long lists in Ionic?

Paginate on the server and load more with ion-infinite-scroll, render only visible rows using Angular CDK virtual scroll, and use track in @for so DOM nodes are reused. Combine with OnPush/signals, lazy-loaded images and pull-to-refresh (ion-refresher) rather than auto-reloading everything.
How do you handle the Android hardware back button?

Ionic handles it by default for navigation, overlays and menus. For custom behaviour (e.g. confirm before exit), subscribe to platform.backButton.subscribeWithPriority(10, () => ...) or use App.addListener('backButton', ...) from @capacitor/app, and call App.exitApp() when appropriate.
Can an Ionic app be a PWA? What are the limitations?

Yes. Add @angular/pwa for a service worker and manifest, deploy to an HTTPS host, and users can install it from the browser with offline support. Limitations: restricted native API access (Bluetooth, some background tasks and full push support vary by platform, especially iOS Safari), no app store presence by default, and storage that the browser may evict. Capacitor builds fill these gaps from the same code.
How do you debug an Ionic app on a device?

For Android, open chrome://inspect in Chrome on the desktop to attach DevTools to the WebView; for iOS, enable Web Inspector on the device and use Safari's Develop menu. Native logs appear in Android Studio Logcat and the Xcode console. Use ionic serve in the browser for fast UI iteration and live reload (npx cap run android -l --external) on real devices.
Why do API calls work in the browser but fail with CORS errors on the device?

In the native app, the web code is served from a local origin: capacitor://localhost on iOS and https://localhost (Capacitor 6+ default; older versions used http://localhost) on Android. To the Spring Boot API these are cross-origin, so add them to allowedOrigins. Alternatively, enable CapacitorHttp, which patches fetch/XHR to make requests from native code, so CORS does not apply; cookies and some interceptors behave differently with it, so test carefully.
How do you write a custom Capacitor plugin?

Generate one with npm init @capacitor/plugin. You define a TypeScript interface, implement it in Kotlin/Java (a class extending Plugin with @CapacitorPlugin and methods annotated @PluginMethod that call call.resolve(...)) and in Swift, plus an optional web implementation. In the app, registerPlugin<MyPlugin>('MyPlugin') returns a typed proxy, and every call is an async promise across the bridge. For a quick app-only plugin you can put the native class directly in the app's Android/iOS project.
How do you test an Ionic Angular app?

Unit tests for components and services work exactly as in Angular (Jasmine/Karma or Jest/Vitest). Mock Capacitor plugins, because they do not run in a test browser: wrap them in your own Angular service and provide a fake. End-to-end tests of the web build run with Cypress or Playwright in a mobile viewport. For real device behaviour (permissions, camera, push), use Appium or manual testing on devices and emulators, plus internal test tracks and TestFlight before release.
How would you make an Ionic app work offline and sync later?

Cache the app shell (it is already bundled locally in a native app; a service worker does this for a PWA). Store data locally in SQLite (a Capacitor SQLite plugin) or IndexedDB rather than Preferences, which is for small key-value settings. Queue writes made offline in a local outbox table with a client-generated ID, and replay them when @capacitor/network reports a connection. The Spring Boot API should treat that ID as an idempotency key and detect conflicts, for example with a version number, so replays do not create duplicates.
How do you handle runtime permissions (camera, location) properly?

Ask just in time, when the user taps the feature, not at startup, and explain why first. Call checkPermissions(), then requestPermissions() if the state is prompt. If it is denied, the OS will not show the dialog again, so show a message with a button that opens the app settings. Declare permissions in AndroidManifest.xml and the usage description strings in iOS Info.plist; a missing iOS description crashes the app when the permission is requested.
What security measures matter for a hybrid app that shows sensitive data?

Everything in the web bundle can be extracted from the APK/IPA, so never ship secrets (API keys with write access, client secrets). Use PKCE login in the system browser, keep tokens in Keychain/Keystore, enforce HTTPS, and consider certificate pinning for high-risk apps. Turn off WebView debugging in release builds, enable code shrinking/obfuscation for native code, and optionally detect rooted or jailbroken devices. Hide sensitive screens in the app switcher snapshot and avoid sensitive text in push notifications. The server must still enforce all authorisation.
When would you not choose Ionic for a mobile app?

When the app is dominated by heavy graphics or animation (games, AR, complex real-time video), needs deep integration with many platform features that have no maintained plugins, or must feel exactly like each platform's latest native UI at all times. In those cases native (Kotlin/Swift), Flutter or React Native fit better. Ionic is strong when a team already knows Angular, the app is mostly forms, lists and API calls, and sharing one codebase across Android, iOS and the web matters.
ion-modal vs ion-popover vs ion-action-sheet vs ion-alert vs ion-toast?

Overlay | Use it for | Blocks the page? | Example
ion-modal | A full task or form on top of the page | Yes | Add allergy form, sheet modal with breakpoints
ion-popover | Small content anchored to a trigger | Yes, dismissed by tapping outside | Overflow menu next to a button
ion-action-sheet | A short list of actions from the bottom | Yes | Take photo / Choose from gallery / Cancel
ion-alert | Confirm, warn or ask for a small input | Yes | "Discard unsaved notes?"
ion-toast | Short feedback that disappears | No | "Saved" after a request
Rule of thumb: the more the user must decide, the heavier the overlay. Never use an alert for plain success feedback; use a toast.
Angular HttpClient vs CapacitorHttp for calling the back end?

| HttpClient (in the WebView) | CapacitorHttp (native)
Where the request runs | WebView networking | Native Android / iOS HTTP stack
CORS applies | Yes | No (not a browser request)
Interceptors, RxJS | Yes | Only if CapacitorHttp is enabled to patch fetch/XHR, which HttpClient then uses
Works in ionic serve / PWA | Yes | Falls back to normal web requests
Typical reason to choose | Default for most apps | Third-party APIs you cannot change CORS on
Rule of thumb: keep HttpClient and fix CORS on your own Spring Boot API; reach for native HTTP only for servers you do not control.
Push notifications vs local notifications?

| Push (@capacitor/push-notifications) | Local (@capacitor/local-notifications)
Who creates it | Your server via FCM / APNs | The app itself on the device
Needs network | Yes | No
Needs a device token on the server | Yes | No
Arrives when app is closed | Yes | Yes, if scheduled earlier
Example | "New lab result is ready" | "Take your medicine at 8 pm"
Rule of thumb: if the event happens on the server, it is a push; if the app already knows the time, schedule a local notification. In healthcare, keep patient details out of the notification text.
ionic serve vs npx cap run vs live reload on a device?

| ionic serve | npx cap run android / ios | ionic cap run android -l --external
Runs in | Desktop browser | Emulator or device | Emulator or device
Native plugins | Web fallbacks only | Real | Real
Code change | Instant reload | Rebuild and sync again | Instant reload from your dev server
Good for | Layout and logic | Final check of a real build | Daily work on device-only features
Interview tip: live reload loads the app from your machine's IP, so the phone must be on the same network, and the back-end CORS list must allow that dev origin too.
